summary: Octagonal stone light of 1826 on the Hudson at Stony Point; kept 1857-1904 by the widow Nancy Rose; a steel tower replaced it in 1925.

lens.where: museum at Stony Point Battlefield (LighthouseFriends; removed around 2011)

structures.note: Thirty feet tall, blue split stone (LighthouseFriends). Unlit since 1925.
Torn down in 1879 (LighthouseFriends). Replacement dwelling built on the flat land west of the lighthouse.
Fog-bell tower; moved in 1890 to a new tower about 200 yards east, near the water (LighthouseFriends; Tribune gives about an eighth of a mile).
Steel tower built near the shoreline (LighthouseFriends), manually operated until 1973. The Coast Guard flashing light now stands on a skeletal tower at the end of the point (LighthouseFriends).

access.note: Exhibits and a restored interior; grounds open; tower open during tours (LighthouseFriends).

facts.agency: Palisades Interstate Park Commission (owner, per LighthouseFriends); Stony Point Battlefield State Historic Site nearby

events.note: Octagonal stone tower built by Thomas Phillips of New York City for $3,350 (LighthouseFriends).
Lit for the first time on 1 December 1826 by keeper Cornelius W. Lansing.
Robert Parkinson appointed keeper (roster; LighthouseFriends).
Lt. George M. Bache reported the tower in very bad condition, its mortar not hardened (as quoted by LighthouseFriends).
Fifth-order Fresnel lens replaced the lamps and reflectors.
Wooden fog-bell tower added to the station.
Nancy Rose becomes keeper after her husband Alexander Rose's death (roster; LighthouseFriends).
First six-room stone dwelling torn down (LighthouseFriends).
Fog bell moved to a new tower about 200 yards east, near the water (LighthouseFriends). Tribune: about an eighth of a mile nearer the water.
Boat landing near the fog-signal tower completed (Light-House Board report).
Fourth-order Fresnel lens installed (LighthouseFriends).
Red lens lantern put on the bell tower near the water, a lower light (Tribune: last November, i.e. 1902).
Nancy Rose died in office (Evening World, May 1904; roster 1857-1904).
Commissioner of Lighthouses proposed to rebuild the light and fog signal, which were in poor condition.
Keeper Millard Caler rescued two men whose boat overturned about twenty feet from shore (LighthouseFriends).
Keeper Caler put out the beacon for good (LighthouseFriends); the Light-House Society place record gives the years discontinued as 1925-1995.
Steel tower near the shoreline replaced the lighthouse (LighthouseFriends).
Steel tower ended manual operation; the last manned light on the Hudson (LighthouseFriends).
Restoration of the lighthouse began (LighthouseFriends).
Restoration complete 7 October 1995; light activated on solar power, a flash every four seconds (LighthouseFriends).
Fourth-order Fresnel lens placed in the lantern room (LighthouseFriends).
Lens removed around 2011 and put on display in the battlefield museum (LighthouseFriends).

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record says sources differ. LighthouseFriends says the 1826 tower no longer exhibits a light and that the Coast Guard maintains a flashing light on a skeletal tower at the end of the point. The record's 'active' status fits that Coast Guard light, not the unlit 1826 tower.

corrections.why: LighthouseFriends and the USLHS record both describe an octagonal tower of stone.
LighthouseFriends says the fourth-order lens was removed around 2011 and put on display in the battlefield museum. Sources disagree; see notes.

notes_for_editor: (1) The 1979 NRHP nomination (NPGallery 79001626) is not digitised (placeholder PDF). The Hudson River thematic group form (64000561) was read only as its cover and classification block; the building inventory forms are not in the PDF. (2) Tribune OCR of the fog-bell winding interval is garbled; the story now uses the Evening World's clean wording ('three hours and threequarters') for the climbs and drops the Tribune's interval. Open conflicts, left in the story: the Alexander Rose appointment (Tribune spring 1852; roster and LighthouseFriends 1853); Nancy Rose's tenure (Tribune 47 years; Evening World 48); the Poughkeepsie wreck (Tribune: a March night with wind and rain, the year not legible in the OCR; Evening World: on the rock in fog; LighthouseFriends gives no year). Please check the Tribune page image for the wreck year. (3) Lens: LighthouseFriends says removed around 2011 to the battlefield museum; Wikipedia's infobox (not cited) says the current fourth-order lens is on loan from the USCG and the Hudson River Maritime Museum. (4) Focal height: the record's 54 m and USLHS's 178 ft do not fit the 1826 tower (LighthouseFriends gives a 30-ft tower; Wikipedia's infobox gives a 58-ft focal height, not cited). The figure is probably for the Coast Guard light; check the Light List. (5) The 1891 Light-House Board item is cited by scan page 79; the printed page is unconfirmed. (6) Several facts come only from LighthouseFriends (the Bache 1838 quotation, the 56-hour fog watch, the Melinda application, the 1923 rescue). The Bache report itself and the Caler rescue were not read in a primary source. (7) The roster includes keepers and Coast Guard staff after about 1960 (Russell W. Scarlett to Terry Dixon). They appear in the roster only, as the archive publishes them. (8) Sarah Parkinson appears only in the roster. (9) The NRHP thematic nomination (64000561) is undated in the OCR; the story no longer dates it. The event for a 1979 NRHP listing was removed: neither the cited form nor LighthouseFriends gives a listing year. (10) The Evening World footnote now omits the 'night edition' label, which the OCR does not show. (11) The 1915 Commissioner item is in the report labelled fiscal 1915 by the corpus (scan p. 84, printed p. 79); not checked against the report's cover.
